analysis.one_liner: Taxes private equity and hedge fund managers' profit share as ordinary income, not low capital-gains rates.
analysis.headline: A bill backed by 15 Democratic senators to tax fund managers' carried interest as ordinary income was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, the share of investment profits that private equity and hedge fund managers take as pay — called carried interest — is taxed at the lower capital-gains rate instead of the rate paid on wages. This bill would reclassify that profit share as ordinary income, tax gains from selling the interest as ordinary income, apply self-employment taxes to it, and raise the penalty for misreporting it to 40%. Genuine invested capital held by the fund's investors and by the managers themselves would still get capital-gains treatment.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers in general, because shifting fund managers' pay from the roughly 20-24% capital-gains rate to the up-to-37% ordinary rate collects more revenue from a group of very high earners; that revenue could fund public priorities or reduce deficits. Wage earners also benefit symbolically and practically because the bill closes a gap that currently lets investment income from labor-like services be taxed more lightly than a salary.

how_it_helps.text: The bill treats the net capital gain from an 'investment services partnership interest' — the carried interest a manager holds for advising, managing, or financing investments — as ordinary income, ending capital-gains treatment for this performance-based pay [S2] [S3].

Genuine capital is still protected: gains attributable to a partner's 'qualified capital interest' — money actually contributed to the fund — are exempt from the recharacterization, so the bill targets compensation for services rather than returns on invested money [S2] [S3].
Income from carried interests would be counted as net earnings from self-employment, subjecting it to self-employment (Medicare and Social Security) taxes that currently do not apply to it [S2] [S3].

The bill raises the penalty for underpaying tax by failing to treat carried interest as ordinary income to 40%, up from the standard 20%, and tightens reporting and anti-abuse rules for related-party and entity structures [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private equity, hedge fund, real estate, and other investment-fund partners who receive carried interest, who would see their effective tax rate on performance pay rise from the capital-gains rate to ordinary income rates plus self-employment tax.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity and hedge fund partners

drawbacks.text: The bill would raise the top combined tax rate on fund managers' performance income well above the current capital-gains rate and add self-employment tax, which supporters acknowledge will reduce after-tax pay in an industry whose business model is built around that pay structure [S2] [S3].

The rules are technically dense — valuation of partnership interests, allocation between capital and service portions, tiered partnerships, and related-party rules all require Treasury regulations — creating compliance complexity and dispute risk for the IRS and taxpayers [S3].

The bill carves out 'qualified family partnerships' — investment partnerships held within one family that do not hold themselves out publicly as investment advisors — exempting them from the ordinary-income treatment, a carve-out that narrows the tax base [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is a defensible simplification of a widely criticized quirk: pay for managing other people's money taxed as if it were investment return. The main costs fall on a small, very high-earning group, though critics argue higher taxes on fund managers could reduce investment activity, and the bill's complexity and family-partnership carve-out show the drafting needed to survive objections. On balance, the benefit — taxing labor income like labor income — outweighs the costs, but it never got far enough for Congress to weigh them publicly.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and with no hearing, markup, or floor action of any kind, it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Tammy Baldwin introduced the Carried Interest Fairness Act of 2019 in the Senate on March 13, 2019, with 14 Democratic cosponsors [S1] [S3] [S4].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, whose jurisdiction covers tax legislation [S5].

The bill's complete action history contains no further steps — no hearing, no committee markup, no vote, and no floor action — so it never advanced and expired when the 116th Congress ended [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity, hedge fund, and real estate fund partners are better off: by dying without a vote, the bill left in place the current law that taxes their carried interest at capital-gains rates, and no comparable bill advanced in that Congress either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fund managers who kept capital-gains rates

for.name: Sen. Tammy Baldwin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Carried Interest Fairness Act of 2019 in the Senate.

for.name: 14 Democratic senators
for.role: Original cosponsors, including Warren, Merkley, Duckworth, Kaine, Reed, Blumenthal, Gillibrand, Whitehouse, Feinstein, Van Hollen, Klobuchar, Booker, and Hirono
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no Republicans signed on.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and took no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Private equity and hedge fund industry
against.role: Fund managers whose carried interest pay the bill would reclassify
against.what_they_did: The industry has consistently opposed carried-interest tax increases and defends the current capital-gains treatment as essential to investment formation; Congress took no action on the bill.

against.name: Senate Republican majority
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-led Senate never brought it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 supporters — the sponsor and 14 cosponsors — were Democrats, with zero Republican cosponsors, and the Republican-led Senate Finance Committee and Senate floor took no action on the bill.

industries.industry: Private equity and hedge fund managers
industries.note: The bill converts their performance-based pay from capital-gains rates to ordinary income rates plus self-employment tax, directly cutting their after-tax compensation. Their interest in keeping the current treatment runs against taxpayers, who subsidize the lower rate on what is functionally service income.

Rental and investment real estate is a 'specified asset' under the bill, so managers of real estate funds holding carried interests would also lose capital-gains treatment on performance income. The industry benefits from the current rules that the bill would end.

industries.industry: Family investment partnerships and family offices
industries.note: The bill expressly exempts qualified family partnerships — investment partnerships held within one family and not offered to the public — from ordinary-income treatment, preserving their capital-gains benefit while other fund managers lose it. Their gain comes at the cost of a narrower tax base for everyone else.

industries.industry: Law and accounting firms serving investment funds
industries.note: The bill's dense valuation, allocation, and anti-abuse rules would require Treasury regulations and substantial restructuring and compliance work, generating business for tax advisors. That gain comes from complexity, not from any benefit to the public.
